CausalChain: HCC cells secrete exosomal PKM2 -> Exosomal PKM2 is internalized by macrophage precursors/Kupffer cells -> Upregulation of PFKFB3 enhances glycolysis -> Increased glycolytic flux leads to PD-L1 upregulation and M2 polarization -> Hypoxia-induced lactate accumulation and Wnt signaling further reinforce M2 state -> Immunosuppressive TAMs inhibit CD8+ T cell function -> Targeted blockade of PKM2/PFKFB3 axis via precision nanocarriers, combined with microenvironment modulation -> Reprogramming of TAMs to M1 phenotype -> Enhanced CD8+ T cell activity improves tumor control
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that in HCC, the targeted inhibition of the exosomal PKM2–PFKFB3 metabolic axis will reprogram immunosuppressive TAMs into an antitumoral M1 phenotype when combined with therapeutic modulation of the hypoxic lactate and Wnt signaling environment. Specifically, precision nanocarriers engineered for TAM-specific delivery will be used to administer PKM2 inhibitors (or siRNA) alongside PFKFB3 modulators, effectively reducing glycolysis-induced PD-L1 expression. Simultaneously, modulation of the hypoxia-induced lactate accumulation and interference with Wnt signaling will be achieved using adjunct molecular agents. This dual strategy is expected to restore CD8+ T cell function and synergize with immune checkpoint blockade to achieve improved tumor control in HCC. State-of-the-art real-time imaging and biosensors will aid in dynamically assessing metabolic and immunologic changes in the tumor microenvironment, ensuring precise adjustment and optimization of the therapeutic regimen.
Abstract: In hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), tumor-derived exosomes laden with PKM2 orchestrate a metabolic and immunosuppressive cascade by priming macrophage precursors and Kupffer cells to upregulate PFKFB3, thereby amplifying glycolytic flux and promoting PD-L1 expression which drives the M2 polarization of tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs). Concomitantly, a hypoxia-induced lactate-rich milieu synergizes with Wnt signaling to reinforce the M2 phenotype, ultimately inhibiting CD8+ T cell-mediated antitumor immunity. Our revised hypothesis posits that specifically targeting the exosomal PKM2–PFKFB3 axis using advanced, precision-engineered nanocarriers—designed for controlled release and TAM-specific uptake—in combination with modulators of the hypoxic-lactate microenvironment and Wnt pathway, will reprogram TAMs from a pro-tumoral M2 state to an antitumoral M1 phenotype. This metabolic reprogramming is anticipated to diminish glycolysis-driven PD-L1 expression, thereby restoring CD8+ T cell function and enhancing responses to immune checkpoint blockade. Advanced imaging and biosensor technologies will be employed to monitor and fine-tune the therapeutic modulation of these pathways in real time, offering a robust and iterative framework for intervention in the complex HCC microenvironment.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis focused on targeting the exosomal PKM2–PFKFB3 axis using precision nanocarriers to modulate TAM polarization and improve immune responses in HCC. Our revised hypothesis retains the core concept but enhances practical implementability by: (1) explicitly integrating contemporary technology such as advanced nanocarriers with controlled-release and TAM-specific targeting capabilities; (2) incorporating a strategic modulation of the hypoxia-driven lactate milieu and Wnt signaling pathways, thereby addressing the complexity of the tumor microenvironment; and (3) employing state-of-the-art imaging and biosensor technologies to dynamically monitor and optimize the intervention. These enhancements refine the original causal chain by emphasizing targeted delivery, mechanistic clarity, and real-time therapeutic monitoring, thereby bolstering the translational potential of the approach.
